title: Being, Alienation, and Production in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
content: Generative AI tools present an unprecedented means through which the written, informational fruits of past social knowledge production may be accessed, and rapidly deployed to accelerate labor tasks, schoolwork, or the building of understanding. Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT are capable of synthesizing terabytes of information into passable written content at a fraction of the time, expertise, and mental labor once necessary to independent digestion, synthesis, and composition. This new reality has led business leaders and academics to lean into the perceived future represented by these tools, in which their use is either neutral inevitability, or a necessary source of transcendent liberation. In the heat of this zeitgeist, few have critically reckoned with the underlying productive relations represented by these tools at the economic and social levels. Fewer still, have directly confronted the implications towards cognitive labor and mental production posed by emerging research on long-term use of generative tools. The process of LLM-driven production and its widespread deployment across institutions does promote a more efficient form of production. However, the efficiency of this arrangement stems from a diminished instrumentalization of the brain. The form of written mental production represented by partial or full reliance upon LLMs is, by all accounts, an exercise in cognitive disengagement. This exercise, rather than strengthening the brain over the long term, produces structural deficiencies in neural connectivity, diminishing individual capacities of critical and creative thought (Kosmyna et al. 2025, p. 112). Underutilization of the brain breeds reliance upon the tool supposedly made to supplement and extend its labor. This paper approaches generative AI tools on these grounds, through the lens of an extended Marxian theory of alienation. Drawing upon emerging experimental research and heterodox accounts of technological production involving the body and the organs themselves, I argue that the off-loading of the baseline cognitive capacities involved in critical thought, concretized into “intelligent” machinery, constitutes an ongoing estrangement of the individual from her being — or her ability to produce, engage in, and externalize conscious, critical thought. This paper explores larger implications for how we conceptualize production, how we engage with our tools, how our tools shape our understanding, and how the use of our tools reflexively impact our brains and bodies.
